name: Chikungunya

pathogens.why: Severe, often disabling, symmetric small-joint arthralgia accompanying fever in an Aedes-endemic area and season is the clinical hallmark of chikungunya, distinguishing it from dengue (which favors myalgia/retro-orbital pain over severe arthralgia) and from bacterial causes of joint symptoms (which are typically asymmetric/monoarticular).

investigations.why: Confirms the diagnosis; RT-PCR is most sensitive in the first few days, IgM becomes detectable slightly later.
Co-circulation with dengue is common and clinical distinction is imperfect — concurrent testing avoids missing dengue, which has different monitoring needs.
Typically shows lymphopenia rather than the thrombocytopenia more characteristic of dengue, supporting clinical distinction.

reason: Fever with severe, often symmetric, small-joint polyarthralgia (the hallmark feature distinguishing chikungunya from dengue) is consistent with chikungunya virus infection — another Aedes-transmitted viral illness. Antibiotics have no role. Management is supportive, focused on analgesia, since joint symptoms can persist for weeks to months after the acute febrile illness resolves.

clinicalPearls: Chikungunya virus (CHIKV) is an arthritogenic alphavirus transmitted by Aedes (yellow-fever and Asian tiger) mosquitoes; after a 2-10 day incubation it causes abrupt high fever, sometimes with a saddleback pattern, plus severe arthralgia (Harrison 22e p.1712).

Migratory polyarthritis predominantly involves the small joints of the hands, wrists, ankles, and feet, though larger joints may also be affected; periarticular swelling and immobility are common, while frank effusions are less frequent (Harrison 22e p.1712).

A rash appears at onset or several days in, often coinciding with defervescence around day 2-3, is most intense over trunk and limbs, and may desquamate; children more often develop a bullous rather than maculopapular/petechial rash (Harrison 22e p.1712).

Although petechiae and epistaxis are occasionally seen, CHIKV should not be classified as a cause of viral hemorrhagic fever; older reports of 'chikungunya hemorrhagic fever' largely reflected concurrent dengue coinfection (Harrison 22e p.1712, p.1706).

A recovery period of weeks is common, and a substantial proportion of middle-aged to older patients go on to develop chronic, sometimes disabling arthritis or arthralgia syndromes typically involving the same joints (Harrison 22e p.1712).

Pregnant women are not at increased risk of severe disease, but there is a high risk of maternal-fetal transmission, especially intrapartum, which has occasionally led to fetal death (Harrison 22e p.1712).

A live-attenuated chikungunya vaccine was approved in the United States in 2023 for adults at increased exposure risk and is contraindicated in immunocompromised persons; about 12% of recipients developed chikungunya-like symptoms in trials (Harrison 22e p.1060).
harrison.pathophysiology: CHIKV is an arthropod-borne alphavirus (family Togaviridae) spread by Aedes mosquitoes. It produces an acute febrile illness with prominent joint involvement; rheumatic manifestations span arthralgia with or without inflammatory signs (periarticular redness, swelling, immobility). Adults experience more severe and articular-predominant disease than children. Chronic musculoskeletal sequelae are thought to relate to host factors, with increased risk in patients who have preexisting osteoarthritis, severe acute disease, or the HLA-B27 subtype, and may be associated with cryoglobulins (Harrison 22e p.1712).
infectionMimics: Dengue (co-circulating Aedes-borne flavivirus; may coinfect) (Harrison 22e p.1712, p.1060)
Zika virus infection (Aedes-borne; can also cause joint manifestations) (Harrison 22e p.1712, p.1060)
Other arthritogenic alphaviruses with clinically similar presentations: Ross River virus, Barmah Forest virus, Sindbis virus, o'nyong-nyong virus, Mayaro virus (Harrison 22e p.1712)
redFlags: Cardiorespiratory, neurologic, renal, or ocular complications in severe acute disease (uncommon but reported, typically in hospitalized patients) (Harrison 22e p.1712)
Pregnancy near delivery, given high risk of intrapartum maternal-fetal transmission and reported fetal death (Harrison 22e p.1712)
harrison.prognosis: Life-threatening illness is rare; most patients recover, though recovery may take weeks. A significant fraction of middle-aged to older patients develop chronic, potentially disabling arthritis/arthralgia. Deaths have been reported, typically in the setting of large outbreaks. Children generally have milder disease and are less frequently hospitalized (Harrison 22e p.1712, p.1060).
pitfalls: Do not label CHIKV as a viral hemorrhagic fever despite occasional petechiae/epistaxis; apparent 'hemorrhagic' cases historically reflected concurrent dengue infection (Harrison 22e p.1712, p.1706).
Do not assume severe disease in pregnancy; the principal pregnancy concern is intrapartum vertical transmission rather than maternal severity (Harrison 22e p.1712).
Do not consider the live-attenuated vaccine safe in immunocompromised persons, in whom it is contraindicated (Harrison 22e p.1060).

algorithms.title: Chikungunya: Diagnostic & Clinical Decision Pathway

steps.action: Chikungunya virus (CHIKV) is an arthritogenic alphavirus transmitted by Aedes (yellow-fever and Asian tiger) mosquitoes; after a 2-10 day incubation it causes abrupt high fever, sometimes with a saddleback pattern, plus severe arthralgia
Screen for high-risk signs: Cardiorespiratory, neurologic, renal, or ocular complications in severe acute disease (uncommon but reported, typically in hospitalized patients) (Harrison 22e p.1712)
Targeted workup: Chikungunya IgM serology / RT-PCR (early illness), Dengue NS1/serology (concurrent testing), CBC
Apply evidence-based criteria to classify disease severity and organ dysfunction.

Pitfall avoidance: Do not label CHIKV as a viral hemorrhagic fever despite occasional petechiae/epistaxis; apparent 'hemorrhagic' cases historically reflected concurrent dengue infection (Harrison 22e p.1712, p.1706).
